title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what it means for learning, teaching, and assessment in higher education. The authors are especially concerned with the rapid public attention around generative AI and the possibility that tools like ChatGPT could disrupt traditional written assessments, enable plagiarism, or otherwise change how educators evaluate student work.

The paper does not report a formal empirical study of a school intervention. Instead, it combines a literature review, background discussion of OpenAI and GPT-3/ChatGPT, and the authors’ own exploratory testing of the chatbot with sample prompts. It situates ChatGPT within the broader Artificial Intelligence in Education literature, using Baker and Smith’s student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing framework to discuss possible educational uses.

The context is higher education, with references to university-level learning, teaching, assessment, and writing support. The paper discusses implications for students, teachers, and institutions, including opportunities for AI-assisted feedback and assessment redesign, as well as threats related to academic integrity and the difficulty of reliably detecting AI-generated text. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT is likely to become part of educational practice, but institutions must adapt assessment and policy rather than assume the technology can simply be banned.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational generative AI chatbot built on GPT-family large language models, designed to generate and revise text through natural-language prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper reviews ChatGPT's functionality and uses it sparingly for brainstorming and experimentation, while discussing its implications for higher education assessment, teaching, and learning.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a review/opinion-style paper with desktop analysis and informal experimentation, not a controlled empirical evaluation of ChatGPT in a school implementation setting. It provides no causal evidence on instructional coaching or lesson plan feedback outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues ChatGPT may affect assessment, writing, and teaching practices, but it reports no measured effect sizes or outcome data. Any impact is speculative and based on discussion rather than demonstrated school-based implementation results.
